newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Tax cartrolling.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-Tax cartrolling.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV political correspondent)

"Yikes! This cart's starting to move!" That was the way The Australian's cartoonist, Peter Nicholson, put Prime Minister John Howard's reaction last week as the momentum for genuine tax reform gathered pace following the High Court's decision knocking over A$5 billion in state indirect taxes.
The fact is this week's tax push was a case of the prime minister's ideology overcoming his caution.
After dipping his toe into the tax reform pool back in May, the High Court gave him the springboard to plunge in at the deep end.
"This great adventure" Howard called in on Thursday. He'll be hoping its conclusion is akin to the Pathfinder mission to Mars rather than the search for the Northwest Passage.
His chances of success are much greater than John Hewson's in 1993 or Paul Keating's in 1985, but the pitfalls are huge, nonetheless.
First is the elextorate's enduring suspicion that tax change means a tax rise.

The prime minister has promised that any reform will be revenue neutral. But he'll have to do more than that. That's why the most important point he made at Wednesday's news conference was to declare that he would stick to his commitment not to increase taxes or introduce any new ones in his first term.
His renewed promise puts a floor of credibility under any tax reform programme he presents for the next election.

But it might take even more than that. One possible, but highly problematic idea might be to use the forthcoming premiers conference to extract an undertaking that whatever reforms are agreed the overal tax to GDP ratio will not increase -- and then to include that in a referendum to be conducted at the time of the next election.
It is the one referendum on tax that could succeed and would stymie the Labor Party, but could be difficult if not impossible to frame.
Special pleading is Howard's other big problem -- a problem that begins very close to home.
Deputy Prime Minister and National Party leader Tim Fischer wasted no time reminding everyone that his party's support was conditional on abolition of fuel excise.
Worth A$8 billion a year to the government, abolition would increase a goods and services tax (GST) by no less than four percent.
The fact is mmost farmers are better off with the diesel fuel rebate -- their abiding fear is that the government will eventually abolish it.

Treasury does keep trying to do just that -- and keeps failing. But as neither party can hope to win government without holding a fistful of regional seats, eternal vigilence should guarantee the farmers' favourite subsidy is secure.
Then there's the question of tax minimisation. Extraordinarily, the topic went unmentioned by Howard on Wednesday.
But if ordinary taxpayers are to face price increases because of a GST, then high income earners must expect to make a contribution to.
The Australian Council of Social Services (ACOSS) has made it clear that a crackdown on family trusts and the like is a key condition for its already tender support for tax reform.
Failure to address the icome side of the tax equation would see the welfare lobby run away from reform like Dracula from a stake.
Privately, Treasurer Peter Costello has been making this clear to business. He will also have to convince his coalition colleagues.

More than hald of the government frontbench has trust arrangements. They will have to endose radical changes to their tax treatment. So will business. Otherwise the broad community support for tax reform will evaporate.
That would certainly sink the chances for the changes business needs.
Seared into the treasurer's memory is the Fightback experience.

He thinks business started to run dead when the going got tough. Equally, former Labor prime minister Paul Keating's bitter experience with business and Option C is also a chastening reminder that selfishness can sink sensible tax reform.

The two best things Howard has going for him are last week's High Court decision and Kim Beazley. The High Court has handed the prime minister a real life demonstration of the dangers of Australia's ramshackle, lopsided tax system.
The prospect of big price rises was real. Howard can say it could happen again.
As for Kim Beazley, he's certainly Mr Nice Guy, but he's no Paul Keating. His performance on Wednesday signalled that he hasn't got the stomach for the mother of all scare campaigns.
He may yet develop it, but it would require an unlikely change of character.
Worse for Labor, it is now locked into a position akin to the Hewson opposition's on Mabo. That is, Labor is simply opposed to major tax reform. It's only contribution to the debate is to oppose.
Australian political history says that's enough to kill much-needed tax reform. John Howard will be hoping he can make history rather than become another victim of it.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
